ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Hageman factor (Factor XII) starts the intrinsic coagulation cascade and produces kallikrein, which generates bradykinin, a key mediator of inflammation and vascular permeability.

sections.p: Factor XII is a plasma protein that, when activated by contact with negatively charged surfaces, initiates the intrinsic coagulation pathway and the kallikrein–kinin system.

t.b: Prolonged aPTT with normal clotting time indicates intrinsic pathway abnormality
Low activity confirms Factor XII deficiency

sections.p: Factor XII deficiency is usually asymptomatic; severe deficiency can cause delayed clotting in vitro but rarely bleeding. Overactivation may contribute to inflammation.
b: Severe: prolonged aPTT, possible inflammatory complications

sections.p: Genetic mutations in the F12 gene are the primary cause. Acquired causes include liver disease, pregnancy, and use of anticoagulants.
Most patients are asymptomatic. In rare cases, patients may have recurrent inflammatory episodes or unusual bleeding after surgery.
Confirm deficiency or overactivation with coagulation tests and specific Factor XII activity.
Severe overactivation can lead to excessive bradykinin, causing angioedema or severe inflammation.
Treat underlying cause. For deficiency, monitor but no routine replacement is needed. For overactivation, use bradykinin pathway inhibitors.
Regular monitoring of coagulation profile in patients with known deficiency. Avoid unnecessary invasive procedures.
Factor XI deficiency (hemophilia C) and other intrinsic pathway defects.
Factor XII deficiency prolongs aPTT but does not cause bleeding; normal aPTT does not exclude other intrinsic defects.
b: Prolonged aPTT may be misinterpreted as bleeding risk

faq.q: Does Factor XII deficiency cause bleeding?
faq.a: No, it usually does not cause bleeding despite prolonged aPTT.
Replacement therapy is rarely needed; management focuses on underlying causes.

faq.q: What triggers overactivation of Factor XII?
faq.a: Contact with negatively charged surfaces, trauma, surgery, or inflammatory states can activate Factor XII.

exam: Explain how Factor XII initiates the intrinsic coagulation pathway and the kallikrein–kinin system.
Describe the laboratory findings that differentiate Factor XII deficiency from other intrinsic pathway disorders.
Discuss the clinical significance of prolonged aPTT in a patient with normal bleeding history.
